author: blu
body: The direction a capability entry grants. These keep their spelling because they name a byte position in a file format, but they are a projection of Foreword chapter Capability and no longer a second copy of its numbers. They were written here as literal 0, 1 and 2, matching cap-dir-* and the compiler's own manifest-dir-* by inspection and by nothing else. cap-dir-bits is the only function that ever reads a direction, and its last branch answers readwrite, so a triple that drifted would not have raised anything -- the loader would have expanded a read-only entry into read AND write and granted an authority the binary never asked for.

author: blu
body: Gpu is the FAMILY, and it is a capability in its own right rather than a synonym for one of its members: it grants Gpu.Compute and Gpu.Memory together. Without it a program whose row says [Gpu] -- legal, because the dotted sub-effect lattice has Gpu covering both members -- earned no capability at all: manifest-cap-id did not know the name, the manifest dropped it in silence, and the process was then refused at the port guard and the window guard it had every right to pass. It compiled clean and died at runtime saying nothing. That is the name-in-one-table hazard, pinned by codex/test/cap-gpu-family.

author: blu
body: Camera, Microphone, Location, Sensors and Display are carriable capabilities in their own right: a program declaring the effect earns the bit at boot and at verified load, the same as Gpu or Identity. The effect operations themselves are declared in the foreword but not yet performable (they die at emit with CDX2040), which is open work -- so the capability is honest about authority and silent about behaviour. The point of carrying it now is that the manifest, the boot grant and the loader agree on the name, so making those operations performable later does not have to relive a name being in one table and missing from another.

author: blu
body: Flash is the authority to rewrite the device's own firmware, and it is its own capability for the reason the OTA design gives: firmware that cannot rewrite flash BY TYPE is an evidence claim, and a claim nobody can read is not evidence. It could have been spelled Device.Flash and cost no table at all -- and that is exactly the trap. A dotted name answers to its base (manifest-cap-names), so Device.Flash would have landed in the Device slot, where a UART driver already sits, and the manifest would have said the same word about a program that blinks an LED and a program that can overwrite the image that boots. The whole point of the capability is the distinction, so it gets its own id.

author: blu
body: Audio is the authority to make the machine emit sound, and it is its own capability for the same reason Flash is. It could have been spelled Device.Mmio and cost no table at all, which is what it was: HdaAudio reached the codec through the raw memory-mapped IO effect, so a program that wanted to beep was granted the Device family -- every BAR on the bus, the block device included. The authority to play a note and the authority to drive the disk controller were the same word.

author: blu
body: Sound out is the other half of Microphone. The machine could already carry the right to LISTEN as a single bit while the right to SPEAK cost the whole device surface, which is the wrong way round if either is: a speaker is the less dangerous of the two.
